text: Eidgah or Idgah, also spelled Eid Gah or Id Gah (Persian: عیدگاه "site of Eid [observances]"; Bengali: ঈদগাহ; Punjabi: عید گاہ; Urdu: عید گاہ; Hindi: ईदगाह), is a term in South Asian Islamic culture referring to an open-air enclosure usually situated outside the city or at its outskirts, reserved specifically for Eid prayers on the morning of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha. It is typically a public space not used for prayers during other times of the year. On Eid mornings, Muslims gather at large open grounds to offer special prayers in accordance with the Sunnah (traditions of Muhammad). Although the term Eidgah originated in India, it is now used broadly for the musalla—the open space outside a mosque—or other open areas where Eid prayers are held, due to the absence of a specific Islamic term for such a site. The term is referenced in the famous Bengali poem by Kazi Nazrul Islam, O Mon Romzaner Oi Rozar Sheshe. The first known Eidgah was located nearly 1,000 footsteps from Masjid al Nabawi in the outskirts of Medina. There are several scholarly opinions in Islamic law (Sharia) that prescribe praying at Eidgahs. Notable Eidgahs globally include the Shahi Eidgah, built in 1658 by Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb Alamgir on the outskirts of Shahjahanabad (now the walled city), covering an area of 31,484 square yards (26,325 m²) with surrounding open grounds. The Shahi Eidgah complex spans 283,257 sq ft (26,315.4 m²) and can accommodate 50,000 namazi at any time, featuring main and side gates on all four sides. The Moradabad Eidgah, located near the Moradabad railway station, has a seating capacity of 20,000 and is a historical religious site where local Muslims perform Eid Namaz annually. Gor-E-Shahid Eidgah Maidan in Dinajpur, Bangladesh, is known as Sholakia and is declared the largest Eidgah in Bangladesh. In 2017, it hosted the largest jamaat in Bangladesh, with the number of devotees increasing due to the construction of a 516-foot wide minaret with 52 domes; the main dome (Mehrab) is 47 feet (14 m) high and the minaret is built in 32 arches, with electric lamps connected to each dome. The minaret is entirely ceramic and visible from afar. The Eidgah has an area of about 22 acres (8.9 ha), though its field is known to be 7 acres. In 2019, the 5th Eid-ul-Fitr congregation at Gor-e-Shahid Baro Maidan took place at 8:45 am with 600,000 devotees, with over 500 police deployed for security. The 6th Eid-ul-Azha congregation, the largest of its kind, occurred at 8:30 am with approximately 4 lakh (400,000) devotees. Eidgah Sharif is a Sunni Sufi shrine in Rawalpindi, Pakistan, founded over a century ago and frequented by visitors from around the world, especially during Milaad Paaks—ceremonies featuring sermons and solo a capella recitations by "reciters." At major gatherings like the Urs Paak, over a million visitors gather on the grounds and surrounding streets. Approximately four million followers from Pakistan and 500,000 from the United Kingdom are regular visitors. The custodian, Shaykh Hafiz Muhammad Naqib-Ur Rehman, known as "Pir Sa’ab," and his son Sahibzada Muhammad Hassan Haseeb Ur Rehman, known as "Sa’ab Ji," lead the shrine’s mission. Pir Sa’ab’s ancestors, previous custodians, were all Sufi masters from the lineage of Mughal Emperor Babur. In 1960, the family donated a significant portion of the land used to build Islamabad, located near Rawalpindi.
